games.title: Active or Passive?
games.statutoryRequirement: Pupils should be taught to use passive verbs to affect the presentation of information in a sentence; use of the passive to affect the presentation of information in a sentence [for example, I broke the window in the greenhouse versus The window in the greenhouse was broken (by me)]
games.instruction: Read it, then tap the right answer.
games.hint: Not quite. Ask who is doing the action and where they are in the sentence.

questions.ask: 'The cat chased the mouse.' Active or passive?
'The window was broken by Tom.' Active or passive?
Which is the passive of 'Sam ate the cake.'?
In 'The letter was written by Jo', who did the action?
Which sentence is in the passive voice?
Which sentence is in the active voice?
'The road was closed.' Why might a writer use the passive here?
Which verb makes it passive? 'The ball ___ by Mia.'
Which is the active of 'The play was performed by Year 6.'?
In a passive sentence, the object of the active sentence becomes the ___.

games.title: Same or Opposite?
games.statutoryRequirement: Pupils should be taught to develop their understanding of the concepts set out in English Appendix 2 by: how words are related by meaning as synonyms and antonyms [for example, big, large, little]
games.instruction: Read it, then tap the right answer.
games.hint: Not quite. Synonyms mean the same and antonyms mean the opposite, so try again.

questions.ask: Which is a synonym for 'big'?
Which is an antonym of 'big'?
Which is a synonym for 'brave'?
Which is an antonym of 'generous'?
Which is a synonym for 'begin'?
Which is an antonym of 'ancient'?
'Fragile' and 'delicate' are ___.
'Arrive' and 'depart' are ___.
Which is a synonym for 'furious'?
Which is an antonym of 'scarce'?

games.title: Formal or Chatty?
games.statutoryRequirement: Pupils should be taught to recognise vocabulary and structures that are appropriate for formal speech and writing, including subjunctive forms; the difference between vocabulary typical of informal speech and vocabulary appropriate for formal speech and writing [for example, find out – discover; ask for – request; go in – enter]; structures typical of informal speech and structures appropriate for formal speech and writing [for example, the use of question tags: He's your friend, isn't he?, or the use of subjunctive forms such as If I were or Were they to come in some very formal writing and speech]
games.instruction: Read it, then tap the right answer.
games.hint: Not quite. Think about how you would speak to a friend or write to a head teacher.

questions.ask: Add the question tag: 'He's your friend, ___?'
Add the question tag: 'You can swim, ___?'
Add the question tag: 'They didn't come, ___?'
Add the question tag: 'It's cold today, ___?'
Question tags are typical of ___.
Which is a more formal way to say 'find out'?
Which is a more formal way to say 'ask for'?
Which is a more formal way to say 'go in'?
Which of these is the most formal?
Which of these is informal?

games.title: Semi-Colon Signals
games.statutoryRequirement: Pupils should be taught to use semi-colons, colons or dashes to mark boundaries between independent clauses; use a colon to introduce a list and use semi-colons within lists; punctuate bullet points consistently
games.instruction: Read it, then tap the right answer.
games.hint: Not quite. Think about the job each punctuation mark does, then try again.

questions.ask: Which marks separate items in a list when the items already contain commas?
Which punctuation mark usually introduces a list?
'We visited Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Oslo, Norway.' Why the semi-colons?
'It was late – everyone had gone home.' What does the dash join?
Which mark could replace the dash in 'I was tired – I went to bed.'?
Bullet points in a list should be punctuated ___.
If one bullet point starts with a capital letter, the others should ___.
Bullet points are mostly used to ___.
'Bring: a coat; a hat; boots.' Which mark introduces the list?
Which mark can show the boundary between two independent clauses?

games.title: Layout Lab
games.statutoryRequirement: Pupils should be taught to draft and write by: using a wide range of devices to build cohesion within and across paragraphs; using further organisational and presentational devices to structure text and to guide the reader [for example, headings, bullet points, underlining]; linking ideas across paragraphs using a wider range of cohesive devices: repetition of a word or phrase, grammatical connections [for example, the use of adverbials such as on the other hand, in contrast, or as a consequence], and ellipsis; layout devices [for example, headings, sub-headings, columns, bullets, or tables, to structure text]
games.instruction: Read it, then tap the right answer.
games.hint: Not quite. Think about how the writer links ideas or lays out the page.

questions.ask: 'Sam likes apples and Ali does too.' Which device avoids repeating words?
'I wanted to win, but I didn't.' Which word has been left out at the end?
'Tom can swim, and so can Jo.' Which word is missed out at the end?
Repeating a key word across paragraphs helps to ___.
Which layout device is best for comparing the prices of three toys?
Newspapers often arrange their text in ___.
Which layout device best lists the equipment for an experiment?
Which device tells the reader what a section is about?
'Some animals hunt at night. These animals are nocturnal.' What links them?
Which phrase links paragraphs by showing a contrast?

games.title: Squeeze the Sentence
games.skillName: Expanded noun phrases for concise information
games.statutoryRequirement: Pupils should be taught to draft and write by: using expanded noun phrases to convey complicated information concisely
games.instruction: Read it, then tap the best answer.
games.hint: Not quite. Keep every detail but use as few words as you can.

questions.ask: Shorten: 'There was a dog. It was old. It was grey.'
Shorten: 'a box. It is made of wood. It holds toys.'
Which noun phrase gives the most information concisely?
Shorten: 'a ship that is huge and is made of steel'
Which noun phrase is the most precise for a report?
Shorten: 'a cake that is made of chocolate'
Shorten: 'a coat. It is for rain. It is yellow.'
Shorten: 'trainers that you wear for running and that are new'
Shorten: 'a lamp for the desk that is bright'
Why do writers use expanded noun phrases in non-fiction?
